deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This page sets up a lattice-point / crossing-number device. It is almost certainly intended for a Gauss-lemma-type (Eisenstein-style) proof of a law for biquadratic residues in Z[i]. The worked example is the square spanned by m/(2+i) with m = 5+8i (norm 89, a prime ≡ 1 mod 4), and 2+i has norm 5.

§1 Definition. Let z be a path in the plane with initial point x+iy and end point x'+iy'.
- S z is the signed number of crossings of z with the unit vertical segments from (1+i)P to (1+i)P+i, with P running over Z[i].
- The points (1+i)P are exactly the lattice points (u,v) with u+v even. So in every column x=u the segments [v,v+1] with v ≡ u (mod 2) alternate along the line, and every lattice point is an endpoint of exactly one segment.
- A crossing counts +1 when z 'goes from left to right', −1 in the opposite case.

Gauss's claim for closed z: S z is 'the number of all points inside the figure enclosed by z'.
- My rigorous reading: the net crossing number of a closed curve with a segment equals ±(winding number at the top endpoint − winding number at the bottom endpoint).
- Hence S z = ±(number of interior lattice points with x+y odd − number with x+y even), i.e. ∓Σ(−1)^{x+y} over interior lattice points.
- So it is a parity-weighted count of interior points, not a plain count.

§2. If z' is the reversed path (x'+iy' → x+iy), then S z = −S z'. This is trivial.

§3, §5. Formulas for how S changes when the path is rotated by i and by −i. They are written as S z plus boundary terms: floors [x'/2], [y'/2], [x/2], [y/2], and 'Quadr. ½(x'+iy'), ±½, …', i.e. an indicator or content of a half-unit square with corner at the half-endpoint. The next page defines this precisely as L P = content of the square ½P, ½P−½, ½P−½−½i, ½P−½i, and writes S iz = S z − LP + LP'. Only endpoint data enter, since rotation by i maps the segment system to a complementary or perpendicular system.

§4. S(−z) = S z + [x'] − [x]. My derivation, writing T for the segment family:
- Rotation by π maps T onto the complementary family T^c in each column and reverses the horizontal direction. So S(−z) = −S_{T^c}(z).
- S_T(z) + S_{T^c}(z) is the signed number of crossings of z with the full lines x = integer, which is ±([x'] − [x]).
- Therefore S(−z) = S z ± ([x'] − [x]). Gauss's sign corresponds to counting a crossing positive when z moves in the −x direction, i.e. the segment, read upward, passes from z's left to z's right. This is consistent with his wording.

Worked example (m = 5+8i). The vertices are tabulated as multiples of m/10.
- Corrected values: A=0; B = m(2−i)/10 = 1.8+1.1i; C = m(4−2i)/10 = 3.6+2.2i; D = m/2 = 2.5+4i; E = m(6+2i)/10 = 1.4+5.8i; F = m(4+3i)/10 = −0.4+4.7i; G = m(2+4i)/10 = −2.2+3.6i; H = m(1+2i)/10 = −1.1+1.8i. All the decimal values are arithmetically correct.
- Structure (my analysis): C = m(2−i)/5 = m/(2+i); G = iC; E = C+G.
- So the figure ACEG is the square with vertices 0, m/λ, (1+i)m/λ, i·m/λ for λ = 2+i, of area 89/5.
- B, F, H are the midpoints of AC, EG, GA. D = m/2 lies on side CE (D − C = (1+2i)/10·m = E − D), so D is the midpoint of CE.
- The large drawing shows the lattice with the vertical segments drawn solid and dashed (the two families), marked endpoints, and this square tilted.

'Dec.' line. A decomposition of the boundary count into half-weighted pieces on AB, BC, CD and full pieces on DE, EF, FG, GH, HA, compared with S AD. The idea is to use the rotation formulas §3–5 to relate the sides of the square to one another (each side is i times the previous one). This is the standard trick for evaluating a symmetric lattice count from a fraction of its boundary.

§6. A 'more advantageous' redefinition. Count crossings of z with unit vertical segments x+yi … x+(y+1)i (the reading of the indices is uncertain; possibly 2y … 2y+1). A crossing is positive when, for even x, z goes left to right, or, for odd x, right to left. Then:
- S z = −S z'.
- S iz = S z − Q[(x'+iy')/2, −½, −½i] + Q[(x+iy)/2, −½−½i], with Q the half-square content of the next page.
- S(−z) is left unfinished.

Marginal arithmetic (+7 2/5, +4 2/5, +2 2/5, −7 2/5, +9 2/5, 4/5, 225, 47, 74, 145) is scratch work. It is partly coordinate sums and partly perhaps related to the accounts on the next page; I cannot interpret it reliably.
errors: §1: for a closed curve the defined S z is not the plain number of enclosed lattice points. Each lattice point is an endpoint of exactly one segment, so S z = ±(#interior points with x+y odd − #with x+y even). Gauss's verbal gloss 'Anzahl der sämmtlichen Puncte' is at best a loose description of this parity-weighted count, unless the point set intended is a sublattice not stated.

§4 sign: the sign of [x'] − [x] depends on the left/right convention. It is correct if a crossing is positive when z moves in the −x direction (segment passes from z's left to z's right), and the opposite sign holds under the other reading. This is not an error but a convention that has to be fixed.

§6: if literally all segments x+yi…x+(y+1)i are used with sign (−1)^x, the column sums telescope and every closed curve gives 0. The indices are probably 2y…2y+1 (or similar), which would reproduce the parity-weighted count.
The 'Dec.' line is incomplete or ambiguous (the last term HA is struck/garbled, and '=' vs '−' before SAD is unclear). The relation it asserts cannot be fully verified from the page.

results.what: Signed crossing count of a path with a family of lattice segments, equal for closed curves to a (parity-weighted) count of enclosed lattice points; reduces lattice-point counting to boundary data
results.modern_name: Crossing number / winding-number (ray-casting) form of lattice-point counting; discrete Green/Stokes-type boundary formula
results.usually_credited_to: Lattice-point methods in reciprocity: Eisenstein (1844); boundary/crossing formulations: later (e.g. Busche 1880s–1890s)

results.what: Transformation formulas for S under rotation of the path by i, −1, −i, with correction terms depending only on the endpoints (floors of half-coordinates and half-square contents)
results.modern_name: Rotation-equivariance (reciprocity-type) identities for lattice-point counts in Z[i]

results.what: Worked example: the square with vertices 0, m/(2+i), (1+i)m/(2+i), im/(2+i) for m = 5+8i, decomposed at the side midpoints for applying the rotation formulas
results.modern_name: Gauss-lemma / Eisenstein lattice count for the biquadratic character of 2+i modulo 5+8i
results.usually_credited_to: Eisenstein 1844 (proof of biquadratic reciprocity via the lemma); Gauss claimed a proof but did not publish it

results.what: S z = −S z' for the reversed path
results.modern_name: Orientation reversal of a signed intersection number

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's unpublished work toward biquadratic reciprocity, including Gauss-lemma analogues and lattice counting, is known from the Nachlass (Werke II). This page shows a specific, fairly sophisticated device: signed crossing numbers with lattice segments and rotation-correction formulas, tested on m = 5+8i and the square spanned by m/(2+i). Such a formulation anticipates Eisenstein/Busche-style geometric arguments. Whether exactly this device appears in the published Werke fragments is unclear, so the page counts as a notable unpublished detail rather than a major new result.

G = iC and E = (1+i)C, so ACEG is a square spanned by m/(2+i).
D = m/2 is the midpoint of side CE.
The area of the square ACEG is N(m)/N(2+i) = 89/5.
